title: Bilateral papillitis as the initial presentation of neurosyphilis in a patient previously treated for primary and secondary syphilis
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
case_prompt:
A 60-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a several-month history of bilateral blurry vision, eye pain, redness, photophobia, and floaters, worse in the right eye. His ocular history was unremarkable. He had HIV infection and had been noncompliant with antiretroviral therapy for the past 4 months, and he was recently diagnosed with hepatitis C. He reported a history of unprotected sexual encounters with men; his last sexual partner was over a year ago. Two weeks before presentation, baseline laboratory tests revealed a serum VDRL titer of 1:256 (negative 5 years earlier), a CD4 count of 241 cells/mm3, and high HIV and hepatitis C viral loads. He denied neurologic symptoms, gummatous lesions, or cardiac signs. He received a single dose of intramuscular penicillin and was referred to ophthalmology. He had restarted antiretroviral therapy 1 week before his eye examination.

On ophthalmic examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/50 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye. Anterior segment assessment showed 1+ diffuse non-granulomatous keratic precipitates and 2+ flare with trace cells in both eyes. Dilated fundus examination demonstrated grade 2 optic disc edema in both eyes without evidence of infectious retinitis. Fluorescein angiography revealed early and late hyperfluorescence of both optic discs with low-grade periphlebitis, greater in the left eye than the right. These findings were interpreted as papillitis, possibly related to neurosyphilis. The patient was admitted for further evaluation. On neurologic examination, he had hyperreflexia of the upper and lower extremities and a positive right Babinski sign. A noncontrast CT scan of the head was unremarkable.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Sarcoidosis was considered — “The differential diagnosis for anterior uveitis and papillitis is broad and includes sarcoidosis, leukemia, infectious etiologies such as toxoplasmosis, syphilis and tuberculosis.”  
2. Leukemia was considered — “The differential diagnosis for anterior uveitis and papillitis is broad and includes sarcoidosis, leukemia, infectious etiologies such as toxoplasmosis, syphilis and tuberculosis.”  
3. Toxoplasmosis was considered — “The differential diagnosis for anterior uveitis and papillitis is broad and includes sarcoidosis, leukemia, infectious etiologies such as toxoplasmosis, syphilis and tuberculosis.”  
4. Tuberculosis was considered — “The differential diagnosis for anterior uveitis and papillitis is broad and includes sarcoidosis, leukemia, infectious etiologies such as toxoplasmosis, syphilis and tuberculosis.”  
5. Ocular syphilis was strongly considered given positive serology — “Our patient’s presentation was non-specific, however, in conjunction with his recent positive VDRL, the diagnosis of ocular syphilis should be highly considered and evaluated.”  
6. Neurosyphilis became likely with neurologic signs and the plan for CSF testing — “Based on CDC guidelines at the time of the patient’s diagnosis, any patient with syphilis and uveitis or other ocular manifestations should have a lumbar puncture with CSF examination to evaluate for neurosyphilis.”  
7. Neurosyphilis was confirmed by CSF findings — “The CSF was found to be reactive for VDRL, thus confirming the diagnosis of neurosyphilis…”
